1.pericope_label: The wicked flee when no man pursueth: but the righteous are bold as a lion... Better is the poor that walketh in his uprightness, than he that is perverse in his ways, though he be rich

schools.summary: Delitzsch works the accents and the syntax, defends the received division of the first verse, and rejects an alternative construing of the third that would turn it into a proportion, on the ground that two of its four terms would then collapse together; Ellicott sets the second verse against the regular Davidic succession and reads the double-going of the sixth as a man walking one way while appearing to walk another.

Gill supplies the concrete detail — biblical panics without a pursuer, thirty tyrants at Athens, the oppressor who has risen out of poverty — and holds that a fool is sometimes not to be answered at all, and never in his own manner.

Clarke reasons about states rather than souls, holding that nations must be judged in this world since they cannot be judged as nations in the next, and that a settled constitution protects a ruler; he also imports Warburton's rule that the defender of religion must not copy the insulter's sophistry but must confute him from his own principles. Wesley reduces the paired commands about answering to two glosses and calls the risen poor man the worst of all oppressors.

Henry reads the group as political and pastoral at once — preferment for the worthless as a disorder in the state, guilt as a bailiff at every corner, the leech and the sponge that suck hardest, and the scripture's apparent self-contradiction as practical instruction about when to speak.

debates.question: Whom does honour given to a fool chiefly injure?

positions.view: The man honoured; he uses it unjustly and is confirmed in his own good opinion of himself.
The state; power in such hands discourages virtue and countenances wickedness.

debates.question: How are the opposite commands about answering a fool reconciled?

positions.view: By the two senses of the phrase: entertaining the foolish premise, which levels you with him, and giving folly its due in a short sharp answer.
By occasion: never copy his manner, but answer where silence would be taken for weakness.
By method: do not imitate his sophistry and scurrility, but confute him from his own principles.

debates.question: Why does a land get many princes?

positions.view: Rival claimants at once, or a rapid succession cut short by deposition and death, with new laws and taxes at every change.
Because nations cannot be judged as nations hereafter, God judges them here; a people who think the constitution favours them leave their ruler alone.
The point is illustrated by the northern kingdom's assassinations set against the Davidic line.

outliers.note: Notes an old English rendering that calls the fugitive of the first verse unpitious, and observes that pity once meant piety.
Rejects a construing of the third verse that would make it a four-term proportion, since the comparison would then explain a thing by itself.

themes: The wicked flee when no man pursueth: but the righteous are bold as a lion.
For the transgression of a land many are the princes thereof: but by a man of understanding and knowledge the state thereof shall be prolonged.
A poor man that oppresseth the poor is like a sweeping rain which leaveth no food.
They that forsake the law praise the wicked: but such as keep the law contend with them.
Evil men understand not judgment: but they that seek the Lord understand all things.
Better is the poor that walketh in his uprightness, than he that is perverse in his ways, though he be rich.

7.pericope_label: Whoso keepeth the law is a wise son: but he that is a companion of riotous men shameth his father... When righteous men do rejoice, there is great glory: but when the wicked rise, a man is hidden

schools.summary: Delitzsch distinguishes the two words of the eighth verse as interest in money and interest in kind, notes a marginal reading that softens their doubling, argues that the prayer of the man who stops his ear is condemned precisely as apparent goodness, and glosses the twelfth verse with an Arabic idiom for a festival day; Ellicott reports that the word rendered hidden means literally sought for.

Gill assembles the etymologies of usury — biting in Hebrew, a birth in Greek, an offspring in Latin — insists that the elect cannot finally be led astray, and traces the rich man's self-estimate to flattering dependants.

Clarke breaks off exposition to wish usurers named at every market cross and deported, explains the stopped ear as a deliberate avoidance of knowledge that will not excuse, and dates the two halves of the twelfth verse from two English reigns; Wesley adds short glosses on causing the righteous to stray and on the withdrawal of good men.

Henry supplies the moral consequences at each point — the household discredited by a son's companions, the estate that passes from cruelty to charity, the broken conversation between God's word and man's prayer, the purse-proud man expecting every sheaf to bow to his — and reads the last verse as a description of a nation's health.

debates.question: What does it mean that a man is hidden when the wicked rise?

positions.view: The Hebrew means literally sought for: men conceal themselves from fear and have to be hunted out.
The people are searched, the clause standing over against a first line that describes festival dress.
Good men are thrust into obscurity and withdraw from public business, until it can seem that none are left.

debates.question: Why is the prayer of the man who will not hear the law an abomination?

positions.view: Because his apparent good is as hollow as his evil: he is not the man his prayer represents, and does not want what he asks.
Because communion with God runs both ways, and one who refuses to hear when God calls is justly unheard when he calls.
Because the ignorance is deliberate, and studied ignorance excuses nobody.

outliers.note: Abandons commentary on the eighth verse for an outburst wishing every usurer's name published at every market cross and the men themselves shipped to the far side of the world.
Reads the transfer of ill-got wealth through the parable of the pound taken from the servant who could not use it.

themes: Whoso keepeth the law is a wise son: but he that is a companion of riotous men shameth his father.
He that by usury and unjust gain increaseth his substance, he shall gather it for him that will pity the poor.
He that turneth away his ear from hearing the law, even his prayer shall be abomination.
Whoso causeth the righteous to go astray in an evil way, he shall fall himself into his own pit: but the upright shall have good things in possession.
The rich man is wise in his own conceit; but the poor that hath understanding searcheth him out.
When righteous men do rejoice, there is great glory: but when the wicked rise, a man is hidden.

13.pericope_label: He that covereth his sins shall not prosper: but whoso confesseth and forsaketh them shall have mercy... A man that doeth violence to the blood of any person shall flee to the pit; let no man stay him

schools.summary: Delitzsch holds that the mercy of the thirteenth verse attaches to confession and forsaking together, since remission does not follow acknowledgement without new obedience; he makes sin rather than God the object of the fear in the fourteenth, describes the ranging bear as one driven by extreme hunger, reads the sixteenth as an address rather than a statement, and denies that the participle of the seventeenth can mean anything but oppressed. Ellicott alone qualifies the promised mercy, and reads the same seventeenth verse as guilt of blood borne rather than done.

Gill guards the maxim about covering sin from misuse, excludes the servile fear of wrath from the fourteenth verse in favour of a filial reverence, derives the bear's name from its hungry growl, and reads the murderer as a man pressed and tortured in conscience.

Clarke treats the thirteenth verse as a plain doctrine of conversion within reach of the weakest, and holds that a weak prince gathers wicked ministers and that the mildness of a government measures its ruler's intellect; Wesley glosses the fear as extending to all times and companies, and adds that none should wish the murderer saved from his punishment.

Henry supplies the images and the paradoxes — the concealed distemper that cannot be cured, the happiness of the man who is always afraid, the tyrant belonging among beasts of prey rather than among reasoning creatures, and tyrants as the greatest fools alive, safer as they would be in their subjects' affections than in their fortifications.

positions.view: Mercy, but only where forsaking accompanies acknowledgement.
Pardon, peace of conscience, and ruin prevented.
Complete forgiveness, though the temporal penalty may still fall, and the next temptation will be harder for this yielding.

debates.question: What is feared in the happy fear of the fourteenth verse?

positions.view: Sin and the harm it may bring on the soul, not God directly, against a Jewish commentator who made God the object.
A filial reverence arising from a sense of God's goodness, not the servile fear of wrath, which has torment in it.
One's own insufficiency; the man distrusts himself and therefore expects trouble and seeks help.

debates.question: Does the man of the seventeenth verse do violence or bear guilt?

positions.view: He bears it; the Hebrew form cannot mean oppressing, only oppressed, so the sense is a man burdened with blood upon his soul.
He does it; the murderer is pressed and hunted, whether by conscience or by the avenger.

outliers.note: Reads the sixteenth verse as a warning called out to the prince himself rather than a statement about him, following Heidenheim against the older interpreters.
Reports an old observation about an undersized letter in the Hebrew word for man at the seventeenth verse, read as marking one red with blood.

themes: He that covereth his sins shall not prosper: but whoso confesseth and forsaketh them shall have mercy.
Happy is the man that feareth alway: but he that hardeneth his heart shall fall into mischief.
As a roaring lion, and a ranging bear; so is a wicked ruler over the poor people.
The prince that wanteth understanding is also a great oppressor: but he that hateth covetousness shall prolong his days.
A man that doeth violence to the blood of any person shall flee to the pit; let no man stay him.

18.pericope_label: Whoso walketh uprightly shall be saved: but he that is perverse in his ways shall fall at once... He that rebuketh a man afterwards shall find more favour than he that flattereth with the tongue

schools.summary: Delitzsch presses the adverb of the eighteenth verse to mean a total and immediate collapse, notes the matched verbs of satisfaction in the nineteenth, takes the plural of the faithful man to mark an unbroken rectitude, refuses to read the morsel of bread as the size of a bribe, and rejects every proposal about the disputed word of the twenty-third; Ellicott glosses the double way, the suddenness, and the degradation of cheap servility.

Gill refuses to let uprightness earn the salvation it describes, spells out faithfulness as promises kept and contracts honoured, widens partiality from the courts to assemblies that distinguish rich from poor, and follows the accents in attaching the disputed word of the last verse to the first clause.

Clarke contributes a single decisive line, that the perverse man falls without resource; Wesley defines the faithful man by his transactions, holds that habit cheapens the price at which justice is sold, and makes the evil eye ungenerous as well as envious.

Henry supplies the moral machinery: the man least safe when he feels safest, the idler who seems to court the poverty he gets, the careful refusal to say that haste to be rich cannot be innocent, the judge who ends by selling verdicts for a crust, and the patient who pays his surgeon gladly once the wound is healed.

debates.question: What is the force of the morsel of bread in the twenty-first verse?

positions.view: Not the size of the bribe, which would be too low a conception, but the fact that even a trifle can raise favour or dislike and bend the will from rectitude.
Exactly the size of the bribe; men who once sold equity for a great present end by selling it for a crust.

debates.question: What does the disputed word in the twenty-third verse attach to?

positions.view: To the reprover's rule: he rebukes after God's directions, or after Solomon's example, as the accents and the Targum suggest.
To the man rebuked, who is going backwards; the other proposals — a reference to God, a self-naming teacher, an emendation — all fail.
To the time of the favour: afterwards, when the man reproved comes to his senses.

outliers.note: Illustrates the totality of the sudden fall with a line of Virgil about a man who bit the ground once and died, and cites a Roman anecdote of a tribune who could be hired with a scrap of bread either to speak or to keep silent.
Refuses to let the verse be read as though an upright walk earned salvation, insisting it only describes who is saved, with grace as the moving cause and Christ as the procuring one.

themes: Whoso walketh uprightly shall be saved: but he that is perverse in his ways shall fall at once.
He that tilleth his land shall have plenty of bread: but he that followeth after vain persons shall have poverty enough.
A faithful man shall abound with blessings: but he that maketh haste to be rich shall not be innocent.
To have respect of persons is not good: for for a piece of bread that man will transgress.
He that hasteth to be rich hath an evil eye, and considereth not that poverty shall come upon him.
He that rebuketh a man afterwards shall find more favour than he that flattereth with the tongue.

24.pericope_label: Whoso robbeth his father or his mother, and saith, It is no transgression; the same is the companion of a destroyer... When the wicked rise, men hide themselves: but when they perish, the righteous increase

schools.summary: Delitzsch defines the destroyer as one who ruins from appetite rather than revenge, observes that the biblical writers never place mental events in the head where we would speak of a hot-head, notes that the proverb about trusting one's own heart was placed by catchword, and prefers to read the increase of the righteous as growth rather than as coming forward; Ellicott answers the robber's excuse that a quiet deed is no better than open violence.

Gill reads the enlarged heart as covetousness or as pride that cannot bear contradiction, presses self-trust past the openly self-righteous to a good man relying on his own sincerity, and records an older reading that applies almsgiving to a teacher who withholds no doctrine.

Clarke holds that a parent's property is as much another's, to the child, as a stranger's, so that robbing it adds ingratitude and cruelty to theft, and states in a line that the heart a man trusts will infallibly deceive him; Wesley makes walking wisely a matter of distrusting one's own judgment and taking counsel.

Henry catalogues the ways of robbing a parent and the excuses offered for it, balances the quarrelsome man's leanness against the trusting man's ease, advises the poor man to give out of his little, and reads the closing verse politically, with the wise declining office and good men absconding.

debates.question: What does it mean that the righteous increase when the wicked perish?

positions.view: They multiply and flourish, as plants do once the caterpillars are destroyed; not that they emerge into public view.
Better men are put into the places the wicked held, and countenance religion by example and interest.

debates.question: Whose trust is condemned in the twenty-sixth verse?

positions.view: A false subjectivity; the heart manufactures thoughts of which scripture says nothing good, while wisdom is given from above.
Not only the openly self-righteous but any man leaning on the sincerity of his own heart, as one apostle did.
The man who trusts what is deceitful above all things and has already deceived him repeatedly.
The man who will not distrust his own judgment enough to seek counsel from others and from God.

outliers.note: Pauses over a difference of idiom, that where we would call a quarrelsome man a hot-head the biblical writers never connect the head with spiritual or psychical events.
Turns the promise to the giver into an argument for giving out of a little, on the pattern of the widow whose handful of meal was preserved because she baked the prophet's cake first.

themes: Whoso robbeth his father or his mother, and saith, It is no transgression; the same is the companion of a destroyer.
He that is of a proud heart stirreth up strife: but he that putteth his trust in the Lord shall be made fat.
He that trusteth in his own heart is a fool: but whoso walketh wisely, he shall be delivered.
He that giveth unto the poor shall not lack: but he that hideth his eyes shall have many a curse.
When the wicked rise, men hide themselves: but when they perish, the righteous increase.
